title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context from the previous page. Euler starts from two Euler-type products. The first is pi/4 * 4/3 * 4/5 * 8/7 * 12/11 * 12/13 * ... = 1. In modern terms this is L(1,chi_4) = prod_p (1 - chi_4(p)/p)^{-1} = pi/4, with chi_4 the non-principal character mod 4. The second is pi/2 * 2/3 * 6/5 * 6/7 * 10/11 * 14/13 * ... = 1. This is the E72 product pi/2 = prod_p (1 + chi_4(p)/p)^{-1}, which equals L(2,chi_0)/L(1,chi_4) = (pi^2/8)/(pi/4). Dividing the first by the second and removing the p=3 factor (which is 1/2) gives prod_{p>=5} (p + chi_4(p))/(p - chi_4(p)) = 1. Taking logarithms and expanding log((1+x)/(1-x)) = 2(x + x^3/3 + x^5/5 + ...) with x = chi_4(p)/p, the factor 2 is halved away.

This page. The first display is that expanded identity written prime by prime: rows for p = 5, 7, 11, 13 with signs +, -, -, +, = chi_4(p). Regrouped by powers it reads sum_{k>=0} 1/(2k+1) * sum_{p>=5} chi_4(p)/p^{2k+1} = 0.

Since S := 1/3 - 1/5 + 1/7 + 1/11 - 1/13 - 1/17 + ... = -sum_{p odd} chi_4(p)/p, one gets
S = 1/3 + sum_{k>=1} 1/(2k+1) * sum_{p>=5} chi_4(p)/p^{2k+1}.
This is a rapidly convergent transformation of a very slowly, conditionally convergent prime series. The first correction is (1/3)(1/125 - 1/343 - 1/1331 + 1/2197 + ...) ≈ (1/3)(0.0048) ≈ 0.0016. Hence S ≈ 0.3349 is 'a little larger than 1/3'. This matches the true value 0.33498..., which Euler later computed in E596.

Observatio. Split each odd prime p into (p+1)/2 and (p-1)/2. Use the ratio (larger)/(smaller) for p ≡ 1, 3 mod 8 and its inverse for p ≡ 5, 7 mod 8. The infinite product of these ratios is 1: 2/1 * 2/3 * 3/4 * 6/5 * 6/7 * 9/8 * 10/9 * ... = 1. In modern form this is prod_p (1 + psi(p)/p)/(1 - psi(p)/p) = 1 with psi = chi_{-8} = (-2/.). It is equivalent to L(1,chi_{-8})^2 = (pi/(2 sqrt 2))^2 = pi^2/8 = L(2, principal character mod 8). Hence, by the same logarithm trick, sum_p chi_{-8}(p)/p = -sum_{k>=1} 1/(2k+1) * sum_p chi_{-8}(p)/p^{2k+1} (sum over all odd primes).

Corollarium. Euler tries to express the inner prime sums sum_{p>=5} chi_4(p)/p^n through the closed-form values P = 4Cq^3 = L(3,chi_4) = pi^3/32, Q = 16Eq^5 = L(5,chi_4), R = 64Gq^7 = L(7,chi_4), etc., combined with Euler-product factors (1+1/3^n)(1-1/5^n)(1+1/7^n)... and a correcting series. As printed, the formula is schematic and garbled; see errors.
errors: In the Corollarium the series is printed S = 1/3 - 1/5 + 1/7 - 1/11 + 1/13 - 1/17 + ... (plain alternation). This contradicts the S defined just above (1/3 - 1/5 + 1/7 + 1/11 - 1/13 - 1/17 ...). It is evidently a misprint or slip.

The Corollarium formula cannot be checked as printed. Taken literally, P*(1+1/3^3)(1-1/5^3)(1+1/7^3)... over all primes equals P/L(3,chi_4) = 1. The bracketed correction '-1 + 1/5^3 - 1/7^3 + 1/11^3 - ...' carries signs that do not match chi_4. At best this is a sketch of a first-order relation between sum_p chi(p)/p^n and L(n,chi), with composite-term corrections left unspecified.

Rigour gap: the products used are only conditionally convergent, since they depend on the convergence of sum_p chi(p)/p. Taking logarithms and regrouping is legitimate in hindsight (Mertens / de la Vallée Poussin), but Euler does not justify it.

ideas.what: Convergence-acceleration of sum_p chi_4(p)/p via the identity prod_{p>=5}(p+chi)/(p-chi) = 1 and the log((1+x)/(1-x)) expansion. This gives S = 1/3 + sum_k (1/(2k+1)) sum_{p>=5} chi_4(p)/p^{2k+1}.
ideas.modern_name: Prime sums of Dirichlet characters via logarithms of L-functions (precursor of the Möbius-inversion formula sum_p chi(p)/p^s = sum_k mu(k)/k log L(ks, chi^k))
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E596, 1775/1785) for the evaluation of S ≈ 0.3349816; the general method to later authors (Glaisher, Landau-type prime zeta computations)
ideas.where_published: E596 'De summa seriei ex numeris primis formatae 1/3-1/5+1/7+1/11-1/13-...' (Opuscula analytica II, 1785); the underlying products are in E72

ideas.what: Qualitative estimate that S slightly exceeds 1/3.
ideas.modern_name: Numerical value of the prime Leibniz series, ≈ 0.33498

ideas.what: Mod-8 analogue: prod over odd primes of ((p+1)/(p-1))^{chi_{-8}(p)} = 1, i.e. 2/1 * 2/3 * 3/4 * 6/5 * 6/7 * 9/8 * 10/9 * ... = 1. Equivalent to L(1,chi_{-8})^2 = L(2,chi_0 mod 8) = pi^2/8.
ideas.modern_name: Euler-product identity for the character (-2/p); special-value relation L(1,chi_{-8})^2 = L(2,chi_0)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (implicit in his mod-8 products for pi/(2 sqrt 2)); not usually stated in this 'split p into parts differing by one' form
ideas.where_published: Related mod-8 products appear in E72 and later Euler papers on Leibniz-type series; this exact form is possibly only in the Adversaria

ideas.what: Attempt to express sum_{p>=5} chi_4(p)/p^n through the closed-form values L(n,chi_4) = (Euler numbers) * pi^n.
ideas.modern_name: Relating prime zeta-type sums to L(n,chi) values (inversion of the Euler product)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E596 does this numerically); systematically Glaisher (1891) onwards

missed.claim: The Observatio gives a 'balanced' product equal to exactly 1 for the character chi_{-8}. This works because L(1,chi_{-8})^2 equals the mod-8 value pi^2/8 = L(2,chi_0). In contrast the mod-4 case yields 1/2 and needs the p=3 factor removed. It implies an acceleration formula for sum_p (-2/p)/p analogous to E596. Whether Euler published this mod-8 version is unclear; it seems to survive mainly in this Adversaria fragment.
missed.quote: productum omnium harum fractionum erit =1, hoc est 2/1 · 2/3 · 3/4 · 6/5 · 6/7 · 9/8 · 10/9 etc. =1
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly historical: it shows Euler working with several real characters (mod 4 and mod 8) and with the relation L(1,chi)^2 vs L(2,chi^2) well before Dirichlet. It is not new mathematics.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is essentially the draft of E596's transformation of the signed prime series, which is known and published. The mod-8 'product = 1' observation is a pleasant detail that may be less documented, but it follows routinely from known L-values.
transcription_corrections: Corollarium: the image indeed prints 'S = 1/3 - 1/5 + 1/7 - 1/11 + 1/13 - 1/17 + etc.'; the transcription is faithful, but this is an inconsistency in the original.
The first display's rows run 'etc.' to the right across all four rows, with '= 0' after the brace; the transcription's layout is acceptable.
